documents.title: Teaching with Generative AI
documents.stance_why: The page sets no rule on whether students may use AI. It says CEETL will "center faculty's expertise", recommends transparency "whatever your stance", and cites S25-257, which only requires a syllabus statement on how and why generative AI "can and cannot be used". Decisions are handed to instructors, so the stance is delegates. The Three Laws are a framework, not tiers.
documents.summary: Teaching-center guidance organized around three principles: teach about AI, teach with AI, and protect student learning from shortcuts. It cites the university syllabus policy requiring a generative AI statement but sets no student-use rule, leaving choices to instructors and disciplines. Most content is rationale, faculty practice and resource pointers.

units.why: States the center's guiding principle that AI is approached as "tools" to enhance teaching and equity; it is a principle of the center (admin, general, informs) and nearest to P56 because it sets purpose and principles.
units.anchor: we approach AI and emerging technologies as tools that may be used to enhance teaching
units.fit_note: A teaching-center stance (AI as a tool to enhance teaching and equity), not a formal institution-wide framework.

units.why: "We center faculty's expertise" and "disciplines may vary" place the approach with faculty and disciplines rather than one rule, so P04, as information.
units.anchor: we recognize that disciplines may vary in their approaches to technology

units.why: Reports that faculty are "embedding AI literacy skills and knowledge into their curriculum"; descriptive of faculty practice and coded as curricular AI literacy (P70) because AI literacy is the first item named.
units.anchor: embedding AI literacy skills and knowledge into their curriculum
units.frag_start: Many SF State faculty are reimagining
units.fit_note: The sentence also mentions talking with students about AI and redesigning assignments, which this type does not capture.

units.why: "CEETL recommends transparency with students" asks instructors to be open about their AI stance, which is communicating expectations; P09 is nearest but this is a recommendation, not a statement requirement.
units.anchor: Whatever your stance is with AI, CEETL recommends transparency with students.
units.frag_start: Whatever your stance is with AI
units.fit_note: A recommendation of transparency whatever the stance, not a requirement of a written syllabus statement.

units.why: Cites Course Syllabus Policy #S25-257, which "requires faculty to include" a generative AI statement in the syllabus: a university requirement addressed to faculty at course start, so P09 must.
units.anchor: "A statement as to how and why generative AI tools can and cannot be used"

units.why: The Three Laws are described as "a framework for addressing the use of AI tools in the curriculum at all levels", so a framework with purpose and scope (P56) that does not itself decide whether AI is allowed.
units.anchor: a framework for addressing the use of AI tools in the curriculum at all levels
units.frag_start: Our Three laws are not laws

units.why: Law One "encourages faculty to teach students about Gen AI", including how it works, "its biases and limitations, and its potential harms"; curricular AI literacy (P70), addressed to instructors as encouragement.
units.anchor: encourages faculty to teach students about Gen AI in ways appropriate to their discipline

units.why: Law Two encourages teaching students "to work with AI tools where appropriate" and prepare them with "AI skills and familiarity they may need in the future": effective AI use as a professional skill (P44), conditioned by "where appropriate".
units.anchor: teaching students to work with AI tools where appropriate

units.why: Law Three says to "protect student learning from AI shortcuts by redesigning assignments to make them AI-resistant where possible"; an assignment-redesign instruction (P35) grounded in the learning rationale.
units.anchor: protect student learning from AI shortcuts by redesigning assignments to make them AI-resistant where possible
units.frag_start: The third law encourages faculty to

units.why: Says students "need to build knowledge about AI" including its social, environmental and labor impacts, biases and hallucinations; teaching this is AI literacy (P70).
units.anchor: Students need to build knowledge about AI
units.frag_end: ways of knowing, reasoning, and writing.
units.fit_note: Content centers on harms and bias, which also fits P53.

units.why: Asks faculty to "partner with CEETL as you redesign assignments and activities", i.e. the center offers consultation to instructors, matching P63.
units.anchor: We encourage you to partner with CEETL as you redesign assignments and activities

units.why: The takeaway "Academic integrity should focus on teaching, not policing" states an educative over punitive stance on integrity, matching P68, as a recommendation.
units.anchor: Academic integrity should focus on teaching, not policing
units.frag_start: Academic integrity should focus on teaching

units.why: The same takeaway says to integrate "AI tools as part of professional learning", presenting AI use as professional preparation (P44).
units.anchor: integrating AI tools as part of professional learning
units.frag_start: Academic integrity should focus on teaching

units.why: Describes faculty lessons where students "use Microsoft Copilot to come up with discussion questions"; an example of instructor-designed AI use to build analytic thinking, coded P44 as nearest, though it is an example not a rule.
units.anchor: Ask students to use Microsoft Copilot to come up with discussion questions
units.frag_start: Ask students to use Microsoft Copilot
units.policy: Faculty ask students to use Microsoft Copilot to come up with discussion questions and then rank and rewrite them to develop analytic thinking
units.fit_note: An example of a classroom AI activity, not a rule; Copilot may be a provided tool (P17) but provision is not stated.

units.why: Says faculty "are also exploring the potential for AI to assist them in curricular design", about instructors using AI in their own teaching work (P59), reported as practice.
units.anchor: Faculty are also exploring the potential for AI to assist them in curricular design.

units.why: Discussion-circle takeaway: AI is "prone to hallucinations, requiring instructors to check for misinformation and personalize"; guidance on instructor review of AI output in teaching work (P59) with a verification element.
units.anchor: requiring instructors to check for misinformation and personalize to their course and students

units.why: Records that participants "raised concerns about inputting personal information or student data into AI systems", a privacy concern about faculty use (P50), stated as information only.
units.anchor: concerns about inputting personal information or student data into AI systems

units.why: Reports faculty worry that "over-reliance on AI might undermine the learning process", the rationale that shortcuts displace deeper engagement (P41).
units.anchor: over-reliance on AI might undermine the learning process

units.why: Faculty emphasized the need for guidelines "ensuring students can opt out of AI-based assignments"; an alternatives/access point (P51) stated as a needed guideline.
units.anchor: ensuring students can opt out of AI-based assignments
units.fit_note: Opt-out is about choice, not specifically cost or access.

units.why: The same sentence calls for "acknowledging AI contributions in any scholarly or educational context", a disclosure expectation (P24), framed as a need faculty identified.
units.anchor: acknowledging AI contributions in any scholarly or educational context

units.why: Describes a workshop on "benefits and limitations of using Co-Pilot to enhance teaching materials" with demonstration and critique of output, an example of support for faculty learning AI (P63).
units.anchor: benefits and limitations of using Co-Pilot to enhance teaching materials
units.frag_end: how they use AI in teaching.

units.why: Quote that AI may be "an easy shortcut around the intentional difficulty we know is at the heart of learning" gives the rationale that shortcuts bypass the practice that builds skill (P41).
units.anchor: an easy shortcut around the intentional difficulty we know is at the heart of learning
units.frag_start: Just because AI can be used

units.why: Quote that students "must first learn the basics of a field" before using shortcuts says fundamentals come first, matching P42.
units.anchor: students must first learn the basics of a field in order to achieve long-term success

units.why: States hallucinations are recognized only by "a user who understands the fundamental concepts", so AI output must be checked by informed users (P31).
units.anchor: only a user who understands the fundamental concepts at play can recognize this
units.fit_note: Also supports P42 (novices cannot judge AI output).

units.why: Says "it may make sense to adopt some teaching strategies that avoid AI and assignments that are more AI resistant" where the aim is learning to think; an option for instructors (P35).
units.anchor: teaching strategies that avoid AI and assignments that are more AI resistant
units.frag_start: In these cases, it may make sense

units.why: Warns that outputs can lead to the output "overrides or displaces students' own thinking"; students' own thinking should not be replaced (P32), here stated as rationale.
units.anchor: the output overrides or displaces students' own thinking
units.frag_start: AI tools can produce authoritative-sounding outputs

units.why: Acknowledges faculty want "AI detectors and prohibitive AI policies" yet moves away from "policing student behavior" toward redesigning assignments; coded P35 because redesign is named as the alternative.
units.anchor: shifts us away from policing student behavior as a way to ensure learning
units.fit_note: Also rejects policing and detectors (P60, P39) as the primary strategy, though not as an absolute.

units.why: Frames open-book vs. open-note and take-home vs. in-class choices as protecting learning from shortcuts: assessment format chosen to protect learning (P35).
units.anchor: whether an assessment should be open-book or open-note, take-home or in-class
units.frag_start: Consider the planning that goes into

units.why: Linked resource titles "GPT Detectors Are Biased" and "The Dangers of AI Detectors" point faculty to material that detectors are unreliable and biased (P39); only a reading list, no rule.
units.anchor: GPT Detectors Are Biased
units.fit_note: Resource titles only; no explicit statement that detectors will not be relied on.

units.why: Lists the resource "Teach, don't police, academic integrity", pointing instructors to respond to AI and integrity through teaching rather than policing (P68).
units.anchor: Teach, don’t police, academic integrity

units.why: Invites readers to "join AT and ITS's AI Literacy Program" to learn what the tools can do, an offered AI literacy program (P70).
units.anchor: To learn what these tools can do, join AT and ITS's AI Literacy Program
units.frag_start: To learn what these tools can do
units.fit_note: Addressed to faculty here; the type also covers students and staff.

notes: Only one included document. The page links to a Computer Science Department AI page and the Academic Senate resolution and policy, which were not collected. Resource link titles (e.g. detector articles) are coded as informs only.
